exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with HIV presents with low mood, weight loss, and insomnia – what investigations do you order and why? — Screen HIV viral load, CD4, TB (GeneXpert), thyroid, and metabolic panel to identify reversible causes.

How do you differentiate a depressive episode from adjustment disorder in a patient after a recent bereavement? — Duration >2 weeks, presence of ≥5 DSM‑5 symptoms, and marked functional impairment point to depression.
A patient on rifampicin develops depressive symptoms; which antidepressant is safest and why? — An SSRI such as fluoxetine, because it has minimal CYP450 induction and low cardiac toxicity.
What are the red‑flag features that require urgent psychiatric referral? — Active suicidal plan, psychosis, rapid decline in cognition, or inability to care for self.
Explain the rationale for using psychotherapy in low‑resource settings alongside medication. — It is cost‑effective, improves adherence, and addresses psychosocial stressors common in the region.

A patient with severe depression refuses food and has a BMI of 16 kg/m²; what is your immediate management? — Hospital admission for nutritional support, safety monitoring, and start of antidepressant therapy.
Why is it important to repeat HIV testing after an initial negative result in a high‑risk patient with depression? — Acute seroconversion may be missed; repeat testing after 4 weeks confirms status.
Describe how you would assess suicidality in a busy outpatient clinic. — Ask about thoughts, plan, means, and intent; document response, assess risk level, and arrange urgent follow‑up if needed.
ai.title: Depressive Episode
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: A depressive episode is a period of persistent low mood and loss of interest with functional impairment. Diagnosis follows DSM‑5/ICD‑10 criteria, severity is staged, and many tropical infections can precipitate it.

b: Core symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia, weight change, sleep disturbance, psychomotor change, fatigue, guilt, concentration difficulty, suicidality.
Severity: mild (≤2 symptoms beyond core), moderate (3–4), severe (≥5 or psychotic features).
sections.p: A depressive episode is defined by at least five of nine core symptoms lasting ≥2 weeks, causing distress or impairment. It may be the first presentation of major depressive disorder or occur secondary to medical illness.

b: Common precipitating infections: HIV, TB, malaria, hepatitis B, schistosomiasis.
Medication‑induced depression: isoniazid, interferon, some antiretrovirals.
Social stressors: bereavement, poverty, gender‑based violence.
sections.p: Understanding the biopsychosocial triggers, especially infections common in low‑resource settings, guides work‑up and management.

b: In HIV, depression predicts poor ART adherence.
TB patients with depression have delayed sputum conversion.
Malaria‑related cerebral involvement can mimic depressive symptoms.
sections.p: Depression worsens outcomes of chronic diseases, increases suicide risk, and may be the presenting feature of an underlying infection.

t.b: Excludes electrolyte disturbances that can mimic or worsen depression; low sodium or thyroid dysfunction may be present.
Identifies HIV as a precipitant; a positive result prompts ART and psychosocial support.

b: First‑line antidepressants: SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine) – chosen for safety, low toxicity, and minimal interaction with most anti‑infectives.
Avoid tricyclics in patients with cardiac disease or on anti‑TB drugs due to QT prolongation.
Psychotherapy: brief interpersonal therapy or problem‑solving therapy feasible in low‑resource settings.
Monitor for suicidality weekly for the first month.
If severe with psychotic features or high suicide risk, consider electroconvulsive therapy where available.
sections.p: Treat underlying medical cause first, then initiate evidence‑based antidepressant therapy and psychosocial support.

b: Adjustment disorder – stress‑related, symptoms <6 months, no functional impairment as severe.
Bipolar depression – history of mania/hypomania; ask about elevated mood, decreased need for sleep.
Hypothyroidism – check TSH; physical signs include cold intolerance, dry skin.
sections.p: Conditions that share low mood or fatigue but have distinct management.
